explain.say: Have you ever wondered what a rubbish dump looks like on the inside? A modern one is called a landfill, and it's built like a giant layer cake. Look at the cutaway on the board. The thickest layer is the rubbish itself, squashed flat by heavy machines.

explain.say: See the thin layer of daily cover? Every evening, workers spread soil or a sheet over the day's rubbish, to keep smells in and stop birds, rats and wind spreading it. Why do you think that matters to people living nearby?

explain.say: Now look at the very bottom, the liner. Before any rubbish arrives, the hole is lined with thick clay and strong plastic, so dirty liquid can't leak into the soil and water underground. Just above, the drains collect that dirty liquid, called leachate, to be cleaned.

explain.say: Look at the gas pipes. As food and paper rot slowly without air, they make methane, a gas that can catch fire and warms our planet. Pipes collect it, and some landfills burn it to make electricity. Can you name something that rots in a landfill?

faq.q: What happens to a landfill when it is full?
faq.a: It is sealed with a cap of clay, soil and grass, and watched for many years. Some old landfills become parks or nature areas.
asks: What is built on old landfills?

faq.q: Why does rubbish rot so slowly in landfill?
faq.a: It is squashed tight and buried with little air, water or light, so the tiny living things that break things down work very slowly.
asks: How long does rubbish take to rot in landfill?

faq.a: A mix of mostly methane and carbon dioxide, made as food and paper rot without air. Methane is a strong greenhouse gas, so modern landfills collect it.
The dirty liquid that forms when rainwater trickles through rubbish. Landfills collect it in drains so it can be treated instead of polluting groundwater.
asks: What is the liquid at the bottom of a landfill?

faq.q: Why is the bottom of a landfill lined?
faq.a: The clay and plastic liner stops leachate leaking into soil and underground water, which people may drink.

facts: Landfill gas is mostly methane and carbon dioxide.
Fresh Kills, once a huge landfill on Staten Island, New York, is being turned into a large park.
